metadata.title: Why GPUs Beat CPUs for AI
metadata.topic: GPU vs CPU · THE AI WORKLOAD

beats.narration_text: Every layer of a neural network performs the same core operation: multiply a matrix of inputs by a matrix of weights, add a bias, and apply an activation function. Training means repeating this billions of times across thousands of batches. Inference means running it millions of times per day. The dominant computational cost of any AI workload is matrix multiplication. Understanding that single fact is the key to understanding why GPUs are the hardware of choice for AI.

show.event: the input column of four circles appears, each with its value
the 4×4 weight matrix builds and takes its gold glow
the 'multiply' arrow draws; the output column resolves
'add bias + activate' lands
the counter starts: 1B … 10B … 100B … 1T
the label settles: the dominant cost

beats.narration_text: A modern server CPU has up to 128 high-performance cores. Each core handles complex branching, deep pipelines, and low-latency single-threaded tasks exceptionally well. A GPU takes a different approach. An A100 has 6,912 CUDA cores — individually simpler, but designed to execute the same instruction across thousands of data elements simultaneously. This is the SIMD model: single instruction, multiple data. Matrix multiplication decomposes into thousands of independent multiply-and-accumulate operations — exactly the workload SIMD was built for.

show.event: left: the CPU chip, eight large cores in a 2×4 grid
sixteen operation tokens queue to its left
one core brightens; a token enters, checks, exits — the clock ticks once
the queue drains a tick at a time, the other seven cores idle
right: the GPU chip fills with its dense grid of cores
all sixteen tokens enter at once; every core lights; one tick clears them
the SIMD badge resolves between the two sides

beats.narration_text: Core count alone doesn't determine throughput. The limiting factor is often memory bandwidth — the rate at which data can be delivered to the processing cores. A server CPU reads from DDR5 memory at roughly 50 to 100 gigabytes per second. A GPU like the A100 uses HBM2e — high bandwidth memory — delivering over two terabytes per second. That's a twenty-times advantage. When thousands of cores need continuous data, the memory interface becomes the critical path. Higher bandwidth means those cores spend less time waiting and more time computing.

show.event: top: the DDR5 tube draws; packets begin flowing at a steady pace
its throughput meter fills low — ~100 GB/s
bottom: the HBM2e tube, three times the height, fills with a dense fast stream
its meter fills high — ~2 TB/s
the 20× badge resolves between the two meters
label: memory bandwidth determines sustained throughput

beats.narration_text: GPUs outperform CPUs for AI workloads because of how well their architecture maps to the problem. Neural networks are dominated by matrix multiplication. GPUs provide thousands of cores for parallel execution. High-bandwidth memory keeps those cores supplied with data. And tensor cores accelerate the most critical operation in dedicated hardware. CPUs remain essential for orchestration, data loading, preprocessing, and the control logic that surrounds the compute. The two architectures are complementary — GPUs handle the dense numerical throughput while CPUs manage everything around it.

show.event: the gold bar slides in: matrix multiplication is the dominant cost
the green bar stacks: thousands of cores for parallel execution
the blue bar stacks: high-bandwidth memory interface
the purple bar caps it: dedicated tensor core hardware
all four pulse together once
right: the CPU piece resolves with its four roles
the GPU piece interlocks with it, equal weight, neither diminished
the closing line settles: complementary architectures
